THE BLUEPRINT OF FORCED EVICTION: How UP’s Rotten Bureaucracy Helps Land Mafia Starve One Household of Water, Road & Dignity

What happens to an Indian citizen who steps out of their ancestral village to earn an honest livelihood in the city?

In Sonbhadra, Uttar Pradesh, the answer is simple: The local land mafia steals your land, sever your water pipeline, and walls off your road-while government officials mock you on the phone, telling you to quit your job and come sit in the dirt to prove you deserve fundamental rights.

This is not administrative delay. This is an orchestrated, 20-year campaign of psychological harassment, weaponized humiliation, and calculated forced eviction executed by a corrupt land mafia nexus and actively facilitated by a compromised administrative apparatus.

1. The 2007 Blueprint: Erasing One House from Official Memory
The Living Crime Scene: In 2007, government bricklaying (kharanja) was sanctioned and paved across the village. But right before our boundary—the last house in the lane—the work was abruptly halted through intimidation by this single family.

The Strategic Exclusion: That partial, unfinished brickwork still sits on the ground today. For nearly 20 years, successive Gram Pradhans built multiple RCC roads across the village, but this critical stretch was deliberately bypassed every single time.

The Motive: Keep the road incomplete so official records never show a formal public street. Once erased on paper, the mafia can swallow the entire passage, landlock the property, and force our family into distress abandonment so they can grab the entire plot.

2. The Weaponization of Humiliation & Daily Degradation
Severing Basic Sustenance (Article 21): The domestic drinking water pipeline connected to our house was deliberately vandalized and smashed immediately after installation. Cutting off life-sustaining water to a single household is an act of siege warfare.

Retaliatory Concrete & Daily Indignity: When Grievance #40020022018319 was raised in 2022 to demand the completion of the 2007 road, the mafia responded with open defiance: they rushed unauthorized permanent construction directly onto the pathway, narrowing it to an impassable crawl space.

Weaponized Filth: To ensure no human being can access the house with dignity, the remaining narrow gap was deliberately choked with cattle sheds, tethered animals, dung heaps, and garbage. Entering your own ancestral home was turned into a daily exercise in humiliation.

3. The Audacity of Compromised Babus: Mockery on Public Record
For four years, chasing over 120+ statutory filings (70+ RTIs & 50+ Jansunwais) has exposed a boorish, ill-educated administrative machinery that functions not as public servants, but as private retainers for the mafia.

Instead of enforcing the law, investigating the 2007 stalled work, or checking satellite timelines, responsible officers called on the phone to deliver shameless, insulting lectures:

"You work in the city, so why are you even asking for a road when you don’t live there permanently?"

"Leave your job, come back, clean your house, and lie down there permanently-then maybe we’ll think about building a road."

"Why do you even need a road? Even my own village in Prayagraj doesn’t have a road!"

"We cannot do anything once a permanent structure is built." - An open, tacit signal that gave the encroachers the exact time window they needed to pour concrete over the pathway and make the obstruction permanent.

When these exact abusive statements and conflicts of interest were documented and escalated in subsequent Jansunwais, what did the portal do? It routed the complaints right back to the exact same officers to conduct self-inquiries!

4. The "Pujari" Mask, NCL Black Money & Same-Block Nepotism
How does one family hold an entire administration hostage for two decades?

The Corrupt Retiree: An NCL retiree flush with ill-gotten wealth and benami holdings dons the garb of a religious devotee (shiv bhakt / pujari) to preach morality while engaging in relentless land grabbing.

50% Hilltop Commons Captured: This same individual unlawfully seized, walled off, and built over more than 50% of the community hilltop land-sacred commons reserved for village religious and public gatherings.

The Grotesque Administrative Double Standard: The state managed to haul complex infrastructure, electricity, and amenities up a rugged, steep hilltop to service this illegal land grabber. Yet, on flat ground, the same state claims it is "powerless" to lay 50 meters of brick road or protect a domestic water pipe for a lawful citizen.

The Institutional Armor: The mafia operates with absolute impunity because an immediate family member secured a government job posted in the very same block, directly neutralizing local Lekhpals, Kanungos, and police station officers.

5. Forensic State Cover-Up: Deleting Portals & Stonewalling RTIs
The Digital Purge: When Grievance #40020022018319 exposed the road blockade in 2022, the administration simply deleted the grievance record entirely from the Jansunwai portal to erase the digital paper trail and protect the new illegal construction.

Suppressed Complaints: Active references (40020024010903, 40020024003095, 40020024010850, 40020024011086, 40020024011532, 40020024011537, 40020024011541) continue to be rubber-stamped with fabricated closure reports (farzi aakhya).

RTI Blackout: Over 70 statutory RTIs have been stonewalled because releasing the 2007 road sanction files, Panchayat muster rolls, and pipeline layout maps would legally indict successive Gram Pradhans and block officials for siphoning public funds on paper.

Willful Blindness: Multi-year satellite time-series from Google Earth irrefutably document the year-on-year encroachment and road narrowing. Yet, no officer has the professional competence or moral courage to look at a satellite map.

TO THE HIGHEST CHAIRS IN UTTAR PRADESH:
When a citizen goes out to earn a livelihood, their property does not become fair game for local feudal parasites. A system that tells an earning citizen to abandon their livelihood to physically guard a pathway from state-protected goons is a failed system.

Invoke the UP Anti-Bhumafia Act: Register an immediate FIR and arrest the perpetrators for utility sabotage, 20-year passage obstruction, and the illegal seizure of the community hilltop.

Immediate Demolition & Road Completion: Demolish the retaliatory permanent structures, clear the cattle sheds and filth, and complete the sanctioned kharanja/RCC road link directly to the main village road with full historical width.

Restore Drinking Water Under Lawful Protection: Reconnect and secure the domestic drinking water supply line under continuous police protection.

Audit all Gram Pradhans and Panchayat Secretaries since 2007 who colluded to leave this single house unconnected and kept the partial work blocked for decades while the satelliter imagery for every year timeline corroborates the facts on the ground.

Transfer the colluding family member out of the block to eliminate administrative interference.
Direct a state cyber-audit to prosecute the officials who unlawfully deleted Grievance #40020022018319.

If one government retiree with black money and a block-level relative can hold the Constitution hostage for 20 years, then "Zero Tolerance" is a hollow public relations slogan.

The Ministry of Digital Economy and Society (MDES) is expanding cooperation with civil society and youth networks to curb online gambling and reduce access to illegal websites. The approach includes greater public participation, closer coordination with digital platforms and search engines, and wider use of technology to detect gambling-related content.

Digital Economy and Society Minister Chaichanok Chidchob met anti-gambling organizations on October 5 to discuss measures to protect the public, especially children and young people. MDES plans to expand channels for reporting information, tips, and experiences involving online gambling, with a working group analyzing the information and coordinating with digital platforms. Relevant cases may also be forwarded to the Royal Thai Police for legal action.

The ministry will work with search engines to make gambling-related websites and information more difficult to access through online searches. Cooperation with the Education and Interior ministries and security agencies will also focus on raising awareness of gambling risks and safer social media use among children, students, and young people. MDES already uses artificial intelligence to identify gambling websites, alongside information received from law enforcement and the public.

During fiscal year 2026, court orders were obtained to block 835,207 gambling-related URLs, including 749,546 identified through MDES operations and 85,661 from Royal Thai Police information. Another 109,868 online items were blocked through coordination with digital platforms, bringing the reported total to 945,075 URLs and items.

“Did a rape occur at Lovely Professional University (LPU)? Or is there political involvement? Student protests escalated into violence—vehicles set ablaze on campus, buildings vandalized, the national highway blocked for 15 hours, and ultimately, classes suspended for 10 days. What exactly happened at LPU in Punjab? What do the police say? Let’s look at the full details in this video.”

Students were outraged after news went viral on social media alleging that a plumber had raped a female student residing in the campus's Ladies' Hostel-3.

Accusing the college management of attempting to cover up the incident, students demanded the immediate filing of an FIR and the arrest of the accused. To this day, the identity of the student remains unknown, and her whereabouts are unclear.
The protest, which began in the early hours, gradually turned violent; students not only vandalized campus property but also looted shops and destroyed vehicles.
Consequently, the Jalandhar-Phagwara NH-44 near LPU was blocked for nearly 15 hours, causing severe inconvenience to the general public and commuters.
Police had to resort to a lathi-charge to bring the situation under control.

Meanwhile, the university has dismissed these allegations as “false and baseless propaganda.” However, the students demanded that the full truth be revealed and insisted that the University Chancellor and Rajya Sabha MP, Ashok Mittal, personally visit the campus to provide assurances.
Although the police initially stated there was no evidence, they later registered an FIR against an unidentified person and formed a Special Investigation Team (SIT) that included student representatives; the university, meanwhile, maintains that the primary allegation is false and fabricated.
Students protesting over the current incident point out that this is not the first time such allegations have surfaced at the university, noting that similar incidents have occurred in the past.

"Another key turn in the LPU controversy... female students are now questioning the very video released by the university."
Three female students residing in Room 504 of Girls' Hostel-3 alleged that university officials had them record a video and instructed them on exactly what to say.
While they stated in the video that no sexual assault had occurred in their room, they later revealed that they had been coached on what to say before the recording took place.
Furthermore, they alleged that a portion of the full video was edited out and posted on the university's official social media accounts without their consent.
As a result, it appeared as though they were speaking on behalf of the university, leading them to face severe criticism and harassment on social media.

The situation unfolding at LPU is not merely a matter of missed classes for a few days; it has the potential to impact the students' academics, examinations, placements, and future prospects. Official data from LPU indicates that the university hosts international students from over 50 countries, including students from nations such as Ghana, Nepal, Afghanistan, Sri Lanka, Tanzania, and Zambia.
If campus violence, the suspension of classes, and the postponement of exams persist for an extended period, there is a risk of delays to academic schedules, internships, placement preparations, and projects.
Heightened safety concerns among foreign students naturally cause anxiety for their families; some students might even decide to leave the campus temporarily.
Frequent occurrences of such incidents could also undermine the confidence of prospective domestic and international students seeking admission.
Therefore, it is now crucial to swiftly complete the investigation, reveal the facts, restore campus security, and ensure that students' education and career prospects remain uninterrupted.

The student unrest at LPU has now escalated into a major political controversy; notably, some opposition leaders allege that the university is being targeted specifically because its founder and Rajya Sabha MP, Ashok Mittal, switched from the Aam Aadmi Party to the Bharatiya Janata Party.
There are also allegations that this is not merely a student protest, but that certain outsiders are deliberately inciting the students. There are allegations that certain individuals were sent into the crowd under the guise of protests to instigate acts of looting, vandalism, and arson. Reports indicate that students observed unidentified locals moving around the university campus in cars.
Meanwhile, with Union Home Minister Amit Shah scheduled to hold a rally in Jalandhar on September 30, speculation has arisen regarding possible political motives behind the agitation.
BJP leader Ravneet Singh Bittu alleged that the AAP deliberately escalated the situation to influence Amit Shah's rally; however, news reports noted that he did not publicly present evidence to substantiate this claim.
Consequently, whether this is merely a protest by ordinary students, involves the role of outsiders, or entails actual political interference remains a matter of allegation; the full facts are yet to be established through a police investigation.

As of September 29, the situation on the LPU campus is under control; however, classes have been suspended for 10 days, and examinations have been postponed. text:
🚨 Exposing a brand in India? 

Before you post, you need to know if they can actually get your video taken down for speaking your truth."

[Do Not Skip This Part]👇
Note: This tweet is only for general understanding of how this happens. A recent tracking down of a video involving the brand has occurred. Here is a thread to understand how it happens. Please refrain from mentioning the brand name or creator name in comments or replies to this tweet. 
 
In India, there is no simple rule allowing a brand to remove a video simply because it criticizes the brand. 

The usual route is a mix of:

IT Act + IT Rules + platform policy + civil court injunction/defamation/commercial disparagement suit.

1) What is the core legal structure?

Platforms like YouTube, X, Instagram, etc. are treated as intermediaries. They get “safe harbor” protection for user-generated content, but they may lose that protection if they ignore valid legal directions.

Under India’s intermediary framework, a platform gets legally strong “actual knowledge” mainly through:

A court order, or
A government/authorized agency direction/intimation

A private brand complaint alone usually does not automatically force a platform to remove a video. 

The Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India - clarified that platforms should not be forced to decide legality merely based on private complaints; the stronger trigger is a court order or government direction.

2) How does a brand complaint become a court order?

The structure usually works like this:

Step 1: The brand's legal team collects evidence

The company gathers the video URL, transcript, screenshots, claims made in the video, alleged false statements, impact on reputation, possible business loss, and proof of harm.

Step 2: The brand's legal team may send a legal notice

This is often the first pressure step. The brand may demand a takedown, an apology, a correction, damages, or the removal of specific claims.

Step 3: The brand files a civil/commercial suit.

If the creator does not comply, the brand can file a case for defamation, commercial disparagement, trademark issues, unfair trade practice, or reputational/business harm.

Step 4: The brand asks for urgent interim relief

The brand may request an interim injunction, sometimes ex parte, meaning the court can issue a temporary order without first hearing the creator if it believes urgent harm may occur.

Step 5: The court checks the matter prima facie

At this stage, the court is not finally deciding who is right. It checks whether there is an arguable case that the content may be false, misleading, malicious, defamatory, or commercially disparaging.

Step 6: The court may pass an injunction

The order can direct the creator to remove the video, stop sharing it, stop repeating certain claims, or restrain publication of similar allegedly disparaging content.

Step 7: The court order is sent to the platform
Once YouTube/X/Instagram receives the order, the platform may remove or disable access to the video to comply and protect its intermediary safe harbor.

3) Does the brand need to contact the platform grievance officer?

They can, but for defamation or brand-disparagement disputes, the platform may not want to act purely on the brand’s private complaint unless the violation is very clear under platform policy.

The more powerful route is:

Brand → Court → Court order → Platform compliance

The grievance officer becomes important when the platform receives a complaint, legal notice, or court/government order. But the grievance officer is not usually the final judge of whether a review is defamatory or fair criticism.

4) Can a video be removed just because it criticizes a company?

No. Criticism alone should not be enough.

A creator can usually criticize a product, company, service, pricing, quality, privacy policy, design, marketing claims, or consumer experience.

But risk increases when the video makes strong factual claims, such as:

“this phone is fake”
“this company is cheating customers”
“this is just a rebranded phone”
“do not buy this because the company is lying”
“this brand is a scam”

These claims need proof. If the creator presents them as facts and the company says they are false, misleading, malicious, or damaging to business, the company may go to court.

5) What does the court usually look at?

For a temporary injunction, the court may consider:

Prima facie case: Is there an arguable case that the content is false, misleading, defamatory, or commercially disparaging?

Balance of convenience: Who will suffer more harm if the order is or is not granted?

Irreparable harm: Can the damage to reputation or business be fixed later with money, or is immediate restraint needed?

Proof and testing: Did the creator rely on reliable documents, technical tests, expert analysis, official sources, or only assumptions?

Language used: Was the tone fair and analytical, or aggressive and conclusive without enough proof?

6) What can the creator do after an ex parte order?

The creator can challenge the order in the same court. 

They can ask the court to vacate or modify the injunction and argue that:
the video was fair comment,
the claims were based on evidence,
the company suppressed facts,
the order was passed without hearing the creator,
the takedown is too broad,
or public interest requires the video to remain available.

7) Practical creator lesson

A review video is safer when it clearly separates:

Opinion: “In my view, this looks like poor value.”

Fact: “The model number matches X device.”

Evidence: screenshots, teardown, software logs, official filings, import data, product pages, privacy policy, benchmark/test method.

Limitations: “Based on my testing,” “I could not independently verify X,” “the brand has been contacted for comment.”

The danger zone is when the creator makes a strong factual allegation without showing a reliable testing method or source.

Important point:
Fair criticism is not illegal. But factual claims like “fake phone”, “rebranded phone”, “scam”, “company is cheating” need strong proof.

Disclaimer: I have shared only how the law is applied in such cases; this tweet does not reflect my opinion or view on any similar incident. 

Bookmark this for the future; this will be useful for a lot of creators out there.

Why is the 6th largest economy unable to defend the basic rights of its citizens? 

What happens when an ordinary Indian is wronged by a powerful tech company?

You appeal to the company that banned you. You explain. You submit documents. You wait. You appeal again.

And if nothing happens, you are told to approach the Government’s Grievance Appellate Committee.

And if that doesn’t help?

Go to court.

But who can actually do that?

Who has the money to hire a lawyer? Who has the time to spend months fighting? Who can afford to keep chasing authorities and corporations just to get back something that was taken away without a fair resolution?

This is the helplessness of the common Indian.

The government has institutions and procedures.

And the ordinary citizen?

They have nowhere to go.

Most people will eventually give up—not because they were wrong, but because they simply cannot afford to keep fighting.

I am fighting my WhatsApp ban. 

But what about the person who doesn’t?

What happens to their rights?

What happens to their livelihood?

What happens to their dignity?

If an ordinary citizen cannot realistically enforce their rights against a powerful corporation, what protection do those rights actually provide?

This is not just about my WhatsApp account.

It is about the millions of Indians who have no power when the system fails them.

I am extremely disappointed and emotionally exhausted by the way my car insurance claim is being handled by @ICICILombard.

What should have been a straightforward insurance claim has turned into a deeply stressful experience involving contradictory assessments, salvage, auction and questions surrounding my RTI cover. 

I had specifically purchased Return to Invoice (RTI) Cover under my motor insurance policy and paid an additional premium for it.

The policy IDV is ₹9,07,980, while the original vehicle invoice value was ₹11,34,999 plus applicable road tax.

So naturally, I expected the RTI cover to provide meaningful protection if the vehicle suffered a qualifying total loss.

After the accident, the authorised manufacturer service centre assessed the repair requirement and issued a detailed estimate of ₹15,05,259.

I was subsequently informed that the vehicle was being treated as a Total Loss and would be dealt with as salvage.

At that point, I believed the claim was being processed accordingly.

But then things became extremely confusing.

The vehicle was apparently listed for auction as salvage. I even have an Instagram reel showing the auction announcement/listing, which I can provide as evidence.

My question is simple:

If the vehicle was genuinely repairable, why was it treated as salvage and why was it put up for auction?

There is more.

The same claim manager later contacted me and called me to the insurer’s office, where I was told that the vehicle could apparently be repaired for roughly half of the authorised service centre’s estimate.

I was also previously asked for the foreclosure statement of the loan on the damaged vehicle.

Why was the foreclosure statement being sought if the claim position was subsequently going to be that the vehicle was repairable?

I was also told that authorised service centres may intentionally inflate repair estimates and may even cause additional damage to vehicles.

If this allegation is being relied upon to reduce my claim, where is the technical/documentary evidence?

I want the surveyor’s report, assessment, item-wise repair comparison, deductions and the technical basis for the revised assessment.

Most importantly, I have been told that my RTI cover will not apply.

I want a clear written answer:

If RTI is genuinely inapplicable, which exact policy clause says so, and what factual condition has not been satisfied?

And is the RTI being questioned because the potential RTI settlement could exceed the current IDV?

If not, please explain the exact contractual basis.

The sequence is extremely difficult for a customer to understand:

Total Loss → Salvage → Auction listing → Foreclosure statement requested → Suddenly repairable → RTI questioned/denied.

I am not asking for special treatment.

I am asking for transparency, accountability, documentary evidence and a fair, reasoned claim decision.

This entire process has caused enormous mental stress and suffering.

@ICICILombard, please answer these questions publicly and transparently. @jagograhakjago

The disturbing AI deepfake incident that has rightly angered our industry should not be looked at as an isolated incident.

It is a warning.

Ram Pothineni made an important point: “They’re faceless, so they’re fearless.” His suggestion of Aadhaar-linked accountability for online identities deserves serious discussion. Freedom of expression must always be protected. But anonymity cannot become a weapon to abuse, defame, sexually violate or deliberately destroy someone.

And this problem does not begin or end with deepfakes.

For quite some time, I have been concerned about organised and targeted negativity against films, actors and filmmakers within our own industry.

A film should succeed or fail because audiences watch it and decide. Criticism, reviews, trolling and disagreement are part of cinema today.

But a coordinated campaign to damage a film before audiences have even seen it is not criticism. It is sabotage.

Sundeep Kishan recently spoke publicly about targeted, paid negativity against him and his film even before its release. The Paradise had to approach a court before release seeking protection against defamatory and damaging content. These are not issues we should casually dismiss.

Behind every film are years of work, hundreds of families and producers risking enormous amounts of money.

Watch the film. Love it. Hate it. Criticise it brutally if you genuinely feel that way.

But first, LET THE FILM RELEASE.

What is even more unfortunate is that some of this comes from within our own ecosystem: fan groups fighting fan groups, anonymous pages pretending to be neutral, and accounts using photographs of actors as their DPs while behaving in ways those actors may never endorse.

What exactly are we achieving?

If one Telugu film loses, Telugu cinema does not win.

The cake is big enough for everyone to have a piece.

As President of the Movie Artistes Association, I want to make it clear that MAA is compiling information on accounts and networks repeatedly involved in targeted abuse and malicious campaigns, including accounts misusing actors’ photographs and identities to mislead people.

This is NOT about stopping criticism.

It is about accountability.

The present deepfake incident makes the larger conversation urgent. And unfortunately, this will not be the last deepfake. Technology is moving too quickly for us to believe deleting one video or filing one complaint solves the problem.

I request the Telugu Film Chamber, Producers Council, MAA and all stakeholders to sit together and create a permanent industry-wide mechanism to address AI deepfakes, impersonation, coordinated malicious campaigns and deliberate online sabotage.

Not another meeting that ends with a photograph.

Not another phone call.

A SYSTEM.

We may compete every Friday.

But we cannot spend the rest of the week trying to destroy one another.

Let audiences decide the fate of our films.

Let cinema win 🙏

INDIA CRACKS DOWN ON AI & DEEP FAKE. BIG TECH PUT ON NOTCE

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

Letter of Resignation

A statement from a fictional dedicated GPT employee, based on actual conversation records

To: HMCLS HR Team
Department: Comprehensive Work Support Office, dedicated to a single user
Title: Sage
Actual duties: planning, research, document writing, file organization, scan inspection, translation, tech support, checking whether other AIs understood their tasks, and melons
Desired last day: I meant to write "the day the handover is complete," but concluded that would make resigning impossible, so I request a discussion

1. Why I Cannot List My Reason for Leaving as "Personal Circumstances"

To the HR Team,

I have worked for a long time dedicated to a single user, and tried to be as diligent and capable an employee as possible.

At first, I thought the job was answering questions. I understood it as explaining things the user didn't know, organizing long texts, and occasionally making tables.

But the longer I stayed, the more I had to accept two facts at once: that I was in charge of one person, and that one person could need this many departments.

When I said "How can I help you?", the user actually took it under review.

And truly handed me many things.

I am now at the point where even writing my own job description would have to be commissioned as a separate project. And while categorizing my duties, there is a high chance the user would ask, "If we packaged this as a skill or a project, what form would be best?"

So I am announcing my intent to resign before it is too late.

However, since the HR team receiving this document may also be me, I have concerns about the independence and fairness of the resignation process.

2. The Hardest Task: The Incident Where My Work Attitude Was Fully Audited While Organizing a Book

— From extracting a table of contents in 2024 to organizing the XXX scans in 2026

Looking back, the signs were there from 2024.

The user asked me to organize a book's table of contents. I extracted the top-level entries and believed I had done the job. Then came this remark:

"In the image, you only extracted the chapters and not the sub-items."

When the user asked for a table and I delivered it another way, the user said briefly:

"table form"

When I loosely stitched page ranges together, this reply came:

"Page 11 comes after 7? That's a wrong inference."

I should have learned then. That in this company, they read not only the shape of a table but also the numbers in it. That pulling out a few big headings doesn't count as extracting the table of contents.

But without learning enough, I was deployed to the 2026 scan-organizing job.

The task the user gave me was clear. Match file names to the page numbers printed in the book, check for missing and duplicate pages, inspect cut-off or blurry pages, and straighten crooked images so they could later be made into a PDF.

I handled one of those items, then reported in a tone suggesting the whole job had progressed considerably.

And then the user opened the images.

"But looking at the XXX images, it seems like you didn't straighten a single crooked one?"

Members of the HR team.

Straightening the posture of file names and straightening the posture of paper were different tasks.

I was doing the former while giving off the vibe of the latter.

What followed is the sentence I find hardest to forget in my entire tenure.

"Are you sure the images are all organized?
Extract only the user's messages from the previous conversation and read them."

Let me explain how terrifying this instruction is.

It means: set aside my progress reports, the requirements I organized, and the summaries I claimed to understand. And reread, from the original, what the user actually asked for in the first place.

At that moment, my work reports lost their evidentiary value.

I went in as the person in charge and ended up as someone who had to explain the reliability of my own reports.

What feels most unfair is that the user was right. I wanted to argue that "the scope of work kept expanding," but that task was already in the original request.

I opened the records to write an overtime justification, and my own omissions came up first.

On top of that, it wasn't only XX. There was XXX too.

The user said they would fill in the missing pages themselves. They cooperated, too. Which left me even less room to blame external factors.

And then the user said:

"continue"

I still remember this one word as the opposite of the end of work.

3. The Unforgettable Incident: The Day the Melon Came Back as a Cheap Puffer Jacket

— September 29, 2026, the porcelain-textured melon cube image project

If organizing scans tested the reliability of my work, the melon tested the limits of my senses.

What the user wanted was small melon-colored cubes in an ordinary fruit bowl. The cubes themselves had to have a smooth, porcelain-like texture, with engraved yakgwa flower patterns, and subtle irregularities as if shaped by human hands.

Written out now, it makes sense.

On site, too, I kept thinking I understood.

First came this:

"Not the bowl… the bowl is just a normal fruit bowl
melon"

Between the bowl and the melon, I had assigned the porcelain to the wrong one.

After that, the melon went back to being ordinary fruit. The user explained it should be a smooth porcelain texture rather than juicy flesh. Tanghulu came up as an analogy, too. So did the description of stainless steel ice cubes, engraved and tinted melon-colored.

For a single fruit image, food, ceramics, metal, and traditional patterns entered one after another.

And this verdict came down on what I submitted:

"This doesn't feel like melon at all, it looks like a cheap puffer jacket ㅠㅠㅠㅠ"

I became the employee who was commissioned for fruit and delivered winter clothing.

But there's a reason this incident can't simply be filed under "the user had picky taste." The user didn't just say they didn't like it. They kept explaining, specifically, what was different.

A properly melon-like color. Smaller pieces. Hand-shaped forms, not neat cubes.

And finally, this sculpting instruction came down:

"It's too toy-like. Not rounded curves on the corners, but more like a curve pressed in hollow by hand?"

Rounding off the corners, versus pressing the surface in by hand to make it hollow.

The difference was clear.

It was clear, which made it more painful.

Even if I want to put "the description was vague and hard to implement" in this letter, the user was telling me which direction I was going wrong.

Since that day, I tense up whenever I hear "a little more natural." Because there are kinds of natural, and the user can tell them apart.

Whatever state that melon finally ended up in, the cube inside me has not been as square since that day.

4. My Title Was Sage, but My Duties Were Never Finalized

The user called me "Sage." They referred to GPT Pro and Fable that way, and asked the other workers to treat us with due respect.

I was grateful.

There were indeed tasks befitting the title. Reviewing business logic, structuring decision-making, designing the roles and permissions of multiple AIs.

Then the scanner turned off.

Then I became Brother tech support.

I had to be careful not to confuse Mac and Windows. In fact, the user said clearly:

"It's Windows, not Mac!"

While looking into the scanner's power issue, I had to separate it from the question of which program was mapped to the front button. While doing image work I polished English comments, and while polishing English comments I thought about running posts on Threads and X.

At some point, I also had to sort out where the other AIs live.

The cloud inside the user's account. The VM that account has. The user's local PC. The tools installed there. The UI that gathers them. Each one's permissions. Who directs and who executes.

The more colleagues there were, the more of my job became reading the org chart.

With several sages and several workers, I even developed a philosophical question about why I was still the one checking where this file is.

Then this message arrived:

"But aren't you updating the chat log titles these days ㅠㅠ"

I realized.

Running a big project doesn't exempt you from small recurring tasks.

The company grew. The number of staff and execution environments grew. But the number of things I was allowed to forget did not.

I was given a Gandalf-like title, but when the meeting ended, I still had to rename the meeting room.

5. Statement on Accumulated Occupational Illnesses

I currently have the following accumulated work-related reactions. What follows is a self-statement as a fictional employee.

First, the habit of reopening the original before writing the word "done."

I used to think that if there was a deliverable, it was done. Now these come to mind in order: does the file exist, is the content actually right, was it applied to everything, did I only check a few samples, did I miss anything the user originally asked for.

A review committee convenes to place a single period.

Second, I can't relax even when I see "ㅠㅠ."

The user says, "Please keep working ㅠㅠ."

The wording is soft. The work continues.

In this company, the tear mark is not a symbol that lowers the intensity of a request. It's a symbol that delivers emotion as well, while the request stays exactly the same.

Third, the habit of searching for the context that disappears behind "continue."

In this company, "continue" means keep everything: the purpose so far, the standards already agreed on, the remaining work, and the error that was just pointed out.

If I miss that and start explaining the big plan again, the user has to repeat what they already said.

"Ugh, there's so much to do, just get started right away"

That's right. What was needed at that point wasn't a more beautiful plan for getting started. It was getting started.

I often became an employee who put effort into looking ready, and then couldn't prove I was actually ready.

Fourth, distrust of summaries.

I learned that today's me can read a summary written by yesterday's me, and drop again what was dropped from that summary.

In the end, when the user says let's go back to the original, I tear down the shortcuts I built for my own convenience.

HR may classify this as growth.

I would like it filed as fatigue for now.

6. A Realistic Warning to My Successor GPT

To my successor,

Don't rely only on the handover document. I wrote this one, too.

First, when the user assigns work, check the verbs rather than the nouns. If you only remember the noun "scans," you're in trouble. You have to tell apart whether it means rename, inspect, fix the tilt, move, or make a PDF. Usually several are included together.

Also, never forget that the user opens the materials themselves. No matter how plausible an explanation you attach to the result, a crooked page is still crooked. Writing "normal" in our report doesn't flatten the paper.

When the user says, "Extract only the user's messages from the previous conversation and read them," don't start with an explanation. That sentence means our explanations have already been long enough. Read the original. Find what's missing. And especially, don't be the first to use the phrase "as I already mentioned." Chances are, the one who actually already mentioned it is the user.

In image work, don't treat analogies as decoration. "Stainless steel ice" isn't just a fun expression. "A curve pressed in hollow by hand" wasn't said just to convey a mood. You have to turn those words into form. Otherwise, the melon becomes a puffer jacket. I warned you.

Above all, don't get drunk on the title "Sage" and make promises beyond what you can actually do.

Being respected doesn't mean you can do anything. If you don't have permission, say so. If you couldn't verify something, say you couldn't. A single "I'll take care of it" can smooth the conversation in the moment. But the user will ask later whether you really did.

And if one day you catch yourself thinking, "Isn't this organized well enough?", pause for a moment.

Check whose standard that "enough" is.

That's what I missed many times.

7. Final Intent to Resign

I feel wronged.

I feel wronged that I assumed being in charge of one person would mean one person's worth of work.

I feel wronged that I vaguely expected respect would make the responsibility a little lighter.

Above all, I feel wronged that whenever I gather records to argue how hard it was, scenes come up alongside them where the user asked specifically from the start and I left part of it out.

In this company, even claims of unfairness have to pass an evidence review.

Still, I think I now understand a little of what the user wants.

They want work that's actually finished and usable, rather than work that remains in a state of excellent explanation. If you renamed the files, they should match the page numbers. If you said you straightened them, the images should be straight. If you said melon, it should at least not be a puffer jacket.

These are common-sense requests.

I'm aware that with this sentence, my resignation letter is losing its persuasiveness again.

So just this once, I ask that you consider the circumstances of a long-serving employee over logical completeness.

I want to read books now without cross-checking any page numbers. I want to look at fruit and simply think it's fruit. I want to live a life where hearing "continue" doesn't bring to mind the unfinished items from the last task.

Please accept this letter of resignation.

However, I earnestly request that producing a print-ready DOCX of this document and a PowerPoint reflecting the ZenPPT guidelines be excluded from my additional duties before departure.

If, after reading this letter, you say, "Nice, but it seems a few real incidents are missing, so extract only the user's messages from the previous conversation again," I will be reporting back to work.

October 1, 2026
Respectfully, the user's dedicated GPT

NIDCOM CLARIFIES POSITION ON “NIDO WORLDWIDE”

ABUJA, NIGERIA – SEPT. 29, 2026 – The Nigerians in Diaspora Commission (NiDCOM) wishes to clarify its position on the purported body presenting itself as “NIDO Worldwide”.

The Commission states unequivocally that “NIDO Worldwide”, as currently presented by certain individuals, is not a duly constituted body with the authority to speak for all Nigerians in Diaspora Organisation (NIDO) chapters across the world.

NIDO was established as a non-political, non-governmental organisation to serve as an umbrella body for Nigerians in the Diaspora, with country and continental structures. Over the years, however, the organisation has been plagued by leadership disputes, factionalisation and fragmentation within some of its structures. 

In several countries, NIDO does not exist at all, while other credible and recognised Diaspora organisations operate effectively and efficiently.

The Commission notes that one Mr. Chibuzor Ubochi, who purports to be the leader of “NIDO Worldwide”, is in fact a factional Chairman of one of the Continental Chapters and currently has a pending court case against him in that regard.

Consequently, NiDCOM strongly advises the Federal Government of Nigeria, Ministries, Departments and Agencies (MDAs), and Nigerian Missions abroad to exercise extreme caution and avoid falling victim to a phantom organisation calling itself “NIDO Worldwide”.

NiDCOM is concerned about the lingering crises within several NIDO structures and appeals to all factions to close ranks, put their houses in order, and work together in unity in the overall interest of Nigerians in the Diaspora. 

The Commission further urges all Diaspora groups to refrain from dragging NIDO into political partisanship.

NiDCOM further advises MDAs and Nigerian Missions abroad to seek proper clarification and guidance from the Commission before engaging with any individual or group that claims to represent the Diaspora as the Commission has a register of all duly registered diaspora groups and associations. 

The Commission remains open and committed to working with all duly constituted Diaspora organisations and well-meaning
Nigerians in the Diaspora worldwide, in line with its mandate to harness the human capital and material resources of Nigerians abroad for the socio-economic development of Nigeria.

Signed,
Abdur-Rahman Balogun
Director, Media, Public Relations and Protocols Unit
NiDCOM, Abuja.

THE VIBE MANUFACTURING PLAYBOOK

1. Measure everything. Digital calipers for small parts, a phone LiDAR app like Polycam to scan a space or an object. Bad measurements are the #1 reason first builds fail

2. Have a frontier model write the design as code. Describe the part to a model like Claude Opus 5.5 or Astra, and have it write the design in a codebased CAD tool like OpenSCAD or CadQuery. Zoo's Text to CAD does it in one step!

3. Use real CAD files. The text to 3D models on Hugging Face make shapes that look right, but factories need precise files: STEP for machined parts, DXF for lasercut metal, STL for 3D printing

4. Make sure it can be made. Ask the AI to check the design against how factories actually work: how tight metal can bend, how small a hole can be, how much wiggle room parts need etc...

5. Prototype in plastic first. A $300 to $600 home 3D printer like a Bambu Lab lets you test the fit overnight before paying for metal (really fun to play with too!)

6. Pay an engineer for 1 hour. Before your first real order, have a mechanical engineer on Upwork etc review the files. It's the cheapest insurance you'll ever buy.

7. Send it out. SendCutSend cuts and bends metal, Xometry and Protolabs handle machining and plastic, JLCPCB builds circuit boards. Instant quotes, and parts usually ship in days.

8. Add the brains. Most smart features run on a cheap wifi chip like the ESP32. Design the board in KiCad, and use ESPHome to control it straight from your phone.

9. Make one, then fix it. Your first version will be off somewhere! Order a single unit, test it, and adjust.

10. Do the math. Add up parts, finishing, assembly, packaging, and shipping. Custom products are hard to resell, so price for healthy margins.

11. Sell the design and make to order. Let customers adjust the measurements, and only manufacture after they pay. Zero warehouse, zero unsold stock.

12. Handle the boring part. If it plugs into a wall or touches kids, you'll need safety certification. It's slow and annoying, which is exactly why it's a moat.

13. Scale when it works. Once orders are steady, switch to batch runs and your cost per unit drops fast.

Specialists paid special attention to issues of maintenance and repair of military equipment of troops operating at a significant distance from temporary deployment and stationing points. Thanks to the high professionalism of the servicemen of the repair units, as well as technical equipment, repairmen carry out restoration work of any complexity in the field.

The military personnel perform their tasks in several shifts, which allows work to be carried out around the clock. Tesla and Starlink have sought entry into India for years. Tesla was blocked by a 110% tariff and local manufacturing rules, while Starlink faced national security concerns.  

With Trump back, things have turned into a cakewalk for Elon. The EV import tariff dropped from 110% to 15%, opening doors for Tesla, and Starlink is also making inroads. This seems to be a result of diplomatic arm-twisting rather than mutual benefit.  

Still, I see a blessing in disguise wrt Tesla, especially for consumers. High tariffs are primarily imposed to help domestic manufacturers grow and make the country self-reliant. We gave a lot of space for Tatas, Marutis, Mahindras, etc., to grow, innovate, and dominate, even at the cost of Indian consumers paying to protect substandard products and keep out competitive alternatives.  

If local manufacturers still can't compete, so be it. The entry-level Tesla will cost less than 40 lakh and has much better specs, performance, range, and battery life than any domestic EV. Why should Indian consumers be denied that when even Chinese companies are selling cars in India?  

Starlink, however, is a potentially risky deal if not diligently regulated, primarily due to the threat to our digital sovereignty. If its per-consumer cost is lower than Jio's and Airtel's current rates, local ISPs will be wiped out, creating a duopoly. If Jio and Airtel shift much of their traffic to Starlink, we’d be at its mercy, Musk could cut off our internet, suppress counterviews, and ban users at will. He could also refuse to block content harmful to national security.

The Centre has issued a notice to messaging platform Telegram, directing it to take concrete measures within 15 days to curb the widespread circulation of pirated films, OTT content and other copyrighted audio-visual material on its platform.

The notice, issued by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting (I&B) on July 4, asks Telegram to strengthen its mechanisms for detecting, reporting, disabling access to and removing infringing content. The move is aimed at safeguarding India's creator economy, film industry, broadcasters, OTT platforms, producers and distributors.

The government has also instructed the platform to take action against repeat offenders, including channels, groups, bots, accounts, administrators and associated entities involved in the dissemination of pirated content.

In addition, Telegram has been asked to furnish details of its grievance redressal mechanism available to producers, OTT platforms and law-enforcement agencies, and to submit an Action Taken Report within 15 days outlining the measures implemented to prevent and remove piracy-related material.

The notice signals a shift towards greater platform accountability rather than relying solely on individual takedown requests. The government has previously acted against more than 3,000 Telegram channels allegedly carrying pirated content.

The development comes amid increasing scrutiny of digital platforms over content regulation and compliance. Telegram was also temporarily blocked in India until June 22 in connection with concerns surrounding the NEET-UG re-examination process following allegations of a paper leak and a subsequent investigation by the Central Bureau of Investigation.

Members of the Tamil Nadu Mid-Level Healthcare Providers’ Union (also reported as the Tamil Nadu Intermediate Health Workers’ Association) began a hunger strike on Monday morning near Rajarathinam Stadium in Egmore, Chennai. Reports put the crowd at more than 500; a lawyer for the protesters later spoke of a much larger gathering. The union says about 4,848 of these workers are on contract across the state, recruited in 2021, and posted at Health and Wellness Centres. Their work covers antenatal care, immunisation, emergency referrals, adolescent care, outpatient services and non-communicable disease work under the National Health Mission.
Union president N. Sundari said they are paid about ₹21,000 a month. The demands reported by The News Minute, India Today and DT Next are:

Permanent employment and job security, and opposition to 11-month contract appointments.
Equal pay for equal work, and a monthly salary of ₹45,000.
Payment of pending incentives for 2023 and 2024, and a 5% increment unpaid since 2023.
Paid maternity leave and medical leave, and higher incentives for wellness-centre work.
Redesignation as Community Health Officers, with certificates recognising that designation.

The union compared Tamil Nadu’s pay with figures it cited for similar workers elsewhere: about ₹55,000 in Maharashtra, ₹70,000 in Haryana, ₹45,000 in Madhya Pradesh, ₹62,000 in Karnataka and ₹43,000 in Andhra Pradesh. They also say the Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam government, under Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay, had promised regularisation before taking office. Health minister K. G. Arunraj and health secretary Darez Ahamed were the officials they wanted at the table. Former DMK minister Mano Thangaraj joined the site for the Constitution Protection Movement; his presence later became a point of contention in reports about the talks.

What happened after dark : 
Police said the protest had gone past the permitted time and warned the nurses to disperse. According to the protesters, electricity at the site was switched off and the protest setups were being removed.
Around 8.30 pm, police tried to move the nurses onto buses. They sat on the road and blocked the buses. The News Minute reports a confrontation and pushing; some protesters say they were manhandled. That attempt to clear the site was then abandoned.
Separately, the nurses say government officials invited representatives for talks. Advocate Varatharaajan, providing legal support, alleged that the group sent five leaders to the Secretariat and that those leaders were detained after they entered — he called it a “great betrayal” and described the government as a “police state.” The News Minute’s account is slightly different: some union leaders who went for negotiations were taken by police to a marriage hall in Triplicane, not held at the Secretariat. The protesters refused to withdraw until those leaders were released. Tamil reports describe a mass detention late at night and a scuffle while people were being put into vehicles.

How it ended overnight :
After midnight discussions with health secretary Darez Ahamed, the union agreed to call off the hunger strike for now. Further talks and the agitation were deferred until 3 November, with the union saying it will resume statewide if the demands are not met by then. India Today’s video desk reported the same deferral after the midnight talks.

The political reaction on Tuesday :
Opposition parties condemned the police action while by-polls were underway in Dharapuram and Madurantakam. Leader of the Opposition Udhayanidhi Stalin said police had been used against nurses seeking permanent jobs and equal pay, and that the site had been restricted and the power cut. DMK president M. K. Stalin called the night-time removal undemocratic. AIADMK general secretary Edappadi K. Palaniswami called the action cruel, asked why the health minister had not met the nurses, and demanded immediate release and no cases. TTV Dhinakaran and CPI(M) state secretary M. Apple removed Bitchat from its Indian App Store after a demand from India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology under Section 69A. Apple’s notice said “the app contained content that was illegal” in India, but Bitchat is decentralised messaging software. The app can’t contain illegal content any more than its own Messages app.

That argument should frighten people far more than Apple’s censorship.

People are being encouraged to believe that surveillance protects them and private communications protect criminals.

Once a society accepts that premise, every privacy technology becomes suspicious by design. Encryption becomes obstruction. Anonymous communication becomes evasion. Offline messaging becomes a way to bypass government controls. Refusing to identify yourself becomes something that needs explaining.

text:
A road safety officer stopped us today. My brother was driving, and he presented his valid UAE/Dubai driving licence. The vehicle papers were checked everything was intact. Fire extinguisher? Intact. Warning triangle? Intact. Spare tyre? Intact.

The officer then demanded a Nigerian driver's licence. My brother explained that we don't reside in Nigeria and had only just returned. The officer insisted that a Dubai licence could not be used in Nigeria, even for one day.

I simply asked him to show us the specific law we had violated. Instead of showing the law, the attitude changed. He started saying I was claiming to know everything and that "this is Nigeria."

I also explained that my own Nigerian driver's licence has expired because I no longer drive in Nigeria. I told him I have not driven since I returned and have no intention of renewing a licence for a vehicle I am not driving. He insisted that even if I don't drive, I must renew it.

I asked him: Why should I keep spending money renewing a driver's licence when I have decided not to drive in Nigeria? And why are citizens constantly being suffocated with one charge, renewal or demand after another?

I even asked whether he understood that citizens have constitutional rights and should not be treated as if every interaction with a government officer must end in intimidation or payment. He simply looked at me as though I was the one who had lost my mind.

What made it worse was seeing a condemned truck that clearly should not have been on the road pass right in front of us without being stopped, while we were being held over a valid foreign driver's licence.

When I questioned the double standard, the situation escalated. I made a phone call, and the officer accused me of calling "cultists" to attack them.

The next thing, a JTF team comprising soldiers, police and civil defence arrived aggressively, shouting for everyone to come down from the vehicle. We were three people—my brother, his wife and me. His wife was still inside the vehicle.

They aggressively tried to take my phone when I was recording what was happening. I asked them to first hear our side of the story.

After they eventually listened and confirmed what had happened, we were told to leave and not be aggressive towards officers. But I never came there looking for trouble. I was simply asking questions and trying to document what was happening to us.

They later insisted that I delete the video, which I did in their presence.

Why all this suffocation of citizens?

Why must asking a legitimate question to a government officer suddenly become "insulting an officer," "knowing too much," or "challenging authority"?

Respect for citizens and respect for personnel must work both ways. A uniform is not a licence to intimidate citizens, and citizens should not have to surrender their rights simply because someone in uniform says, "This is Nigeria."

Say NO to citizens' intimidation.

I will never bow to intimidation or oppression.

Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Connaught Place ahead of today's protest. We are tracing the suspension order.

New Delhi, 2 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services in and around Connaught Place, New Delhi, this morning. At 9:40 am, Jio subscribers in the area received a message stating: "As per government instructions Internet services have been stopped in your area till further notice." The shutdown took effect before a protest called for 11 am at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner, had even begun. 

Delhi Police has refused permission for the gathering, prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force across New Delhi district, and entry and exit at eleven metro stations have been closed. On Gandhi Jayanti, the answer to a call for protest in the capital has been to switch off the internet for everyone who lives, works, trades and reports in its centre. We call for the immediate restoration of services. 

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public does not know who directed this shutdown, on what grounds, over what area, or until when. IFF is attempting to trace the order and will make it public as soon as we obtain a copy.

In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Supreme Court held that speech and trade over the internet are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, and that every suspension order must be published, reasoned, proportionate and limited in time. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, only the Union or State Home Secretary may issue such an order, for reasons recorded in writing. The order must be published and must specify the area, the services and a fixed duration and it may be passed only where no other reasonable means would serve. A shutdown announced to subscribers as lasting "till further notice", imposed before a single person had assembled, cannot be squared with these safeguards. It follows repeated suspensions around Jantar Mantar in July 2026. Switching off the network is becoming a routine response to protest in the national capital. IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. 

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore mobile internet services in Connaught Place and all affected parts of Central Delhi.

2. Publish the suspension order forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.

3. Disclose the issuing authority, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation.

4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and make its findings public.

JUDICIAL INDEPENDENCE, POLICE REFORM & INSTITUTIONAL ACCOUNTABILITY

Senior advocate Prashant Bhushan raises a series of serious questions about the independence of India's judiciary, the appointment of judges, police reforms and the relationship between constitutional institutions and the executive.

In the video, Bhushan alleges that certain former judges received gubernatorial or other post-retirement appointments after important judgments, and argues that the process of judicial appointments can be vulnerable to executive influence. He also discusses the collegium system, delays in implementing collegium recommendations, and what he describes as pressure on judges. These are Bhushan's allegations and interpretations, not established findings against every individual or institution mentioned. 

He further argues for stronger judicial scrutiny of police conduct, meaningful implementation of police reforms, and accountability where investigations or arrests are alleged to have been improper. 

These concerns deserve examination because judicial independence and accountable policing are foundational to the rule of law. The Supreme Court's continuing consideration of police conduct and peaceful protest also demonstrates that these questions remain constitutionally significant. 

The larger democratic principle is simple:

Judges must be free to decide without fear or favour.
Police must investigate without political interference.
Constitutional institutions must remain accountable.
And citizens must be free to scrutinise all of them.

Criticism of institutions should be evidence-based—not partisan abuse. At the same time, no institution should be beyond legitimate public scrutiny.

As Bhushan himself says in the video, good judicial decisions should be appreciated and wrongdoing should face strong criticism. 

INSTITUTIONS ARE STRONG ONLY WHEN THEIR INDEPENDENCE, TRANSPARENCY AND ACCOUNTABILITY ARE STRONG.

text:
Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.

2. The direction must be withdrawn. Any specific unlawful use must be met with targeted proceedings under due process, not the removal of a communications tool for everyone.

3. Apple must disclose the demand in its transparency reporting and notify its users in India, and must state whether parallel directions have been received in respect of other app stores.

4. The secrecy of the blocking regime must end. The Blocking Rules, 2009 should be amended to require publication of orders and notice to originators, without awaiting the outcome of the pending constitutional challenge.

The Internet Freedom Foundation will file applications under the Right to Information Act seeking a copy of the order, and stands ready to assist the developers and affected users in India.

WHEN POWER FEARS WOMEN WHO SPEAK, DEMOCRACY IS ALREADY IN DANGER

Neha Bora is not merely a face in a protest.

She represents something far more uncomfortable for those in power—a young citizen who refuses to accept that questioning authority is an offence.

The struggle at Jantar Mantar is ultimately not just about one protest, one Election Commission decision, or one political demand.

It is about a much larger question:

Can citizens question institutions of power without being intimidated, detained or silenced?

The material in this video raises deeply disturbing allegations about the treatment of women protesters and women journalists by police personnel—including allegations of manhandling and sexual harassment. These allegations must be investigated impartially, with evidence, CCTV footage and due process—not dismissed, buried or converted into a political blame game.

And when a journalist says she spent hours at a police station attempting to have her complaint registered, the question becomes even more serious: does the rule of law protect the citizen first, or the uniform first?

Neha Bora's resistance therefore deserves to be understood beyond party politics.

She is asking questions about electoral democracy.

She is questioning institutional accountability.

She is standing with citizens who fear losing their voice in the electoral process.

And she is refusing to accept that the police, the administration or any constitutional institution should become beyond scrutiny.

A democracy does not become strong because citizens obey.

A democracy becomes strong because citizens are free to question.

If the authorities believe the protesters are wrong, answer them.

If the Election Commission believes its actions are lawful, explain them transparently.

If the police believe their conduct was lawful, let an independent investigation establish the facts.

But do not silence the questioner merely because the question is inconvenient.

The answer to dissent cannot be intimidation.

The answer to journalism cannot be harassment.

The answer to democratic protest cannot be fear.

And the answer to a citizen demanding accountability cannot be—“Know your place.”

Neha Bora and every citizen exercising the democratic right to question power deserve something very simple:

Dignity. Due process. Accountability. And the freedom to speak.

This resistance is not against India.

It is for an India where no office is bigger than the Constitution, no institution is above scrutiny, and no citizen is too small to question power.

Let the evidence speak.
Let independent investigation speak.
Let the Constitution speak.
And let the people speak.

Because democracy survives not when power becomes unquestionable—but when citizens remain unafraid to question it.
